name: Data warehouses
summary: A columnar database for big analytical questions over all your data.
howItWorks: A data warehouse gathers data from many systems and stores it column by column, so a query that averages one field over billions of rows reads only that column. Compute scales separately from storage, and a single query can be spread across hundreds or thousands of CPU cores. A lakehouse applies the same idea to open table formats such as Apache Iceberg sitting in object storage.
analogy: A national library’s research archive. You go there to answer “how has this changed over ten years?”, and nobody expects the answer in a millisecond.
useWhen: BI dashboards and reporting across many sources
Ad-hoc analysis of years of history
avoidWhen: Serving an app’s per-user reads and writes
Real-time lookups that need millisecond latency
example: Hourly jobs load orders, payment events and CSV exports into BigQuery. An analyst joins three years of data to see which regions churned after a price change; the query scans 2 TB, and on demand BigQuery bills for those bytes.

providers.oss: Iceberg + Trino, Apache Hive (and its Metastore, still the catalog many engines use), ClickHouse, DuckDB; also Snowflake, Databricks, MotherDuck (hosted DuckDB), Firebolt, Alibaba Cloud Hologres

diagram.caption: Load jobs pull data from three sources into the warehouse. An analyst’s query takes longer than an app lookup, but it can cover everything at once.

story: In the 1970s and early 1980s, companies ran their business on operational systems: order entry, billing, inventory. To ask a question across them, such as sales by region over five years, large companies ran several decision-support environments side by side, each repeating the work of gathering, cleaning and integrating the same data from those systems. Long analytical queries run directly on transaction databases also caused lock contention. Teradata’s DBC/1012 (1983) was one of the first machines built specifically for decision support.

In 1988, Barry Devlin and Paul Murphy of IBM described a “business data warehouse”: one integrated copy of the company’s data, loaded from the operational systems and kept for analysis. Bill Inmon’s 1992 book Building the Data Warehouse and Ralph Kimball’s 1996 The Data Warehouse Toolkit, with its star schemas of facts and dimensions, set the two main schools of design. Storage changed too: column stores such as Sybase IQ and the 2005 C-Store research system (which became Vertica) showed that reading only the needed columns made warehouse queries far faster.

The cloud removed the hardware. Google’s BigQuery (2010), Amazon Redshift (2012) and Snowflake (2015) sold warehouses as services, Redshift at under $1,000 per terabyte per year against $19,000 to $25,000 for a traditional one. Around 2020 the lakehouse idea brought the same features to open files in object storage.

choices.choice: A separate copy of data for analysis
choices.why: Every decision-support group was rebuilding the same extracts, and long analytical queries held locks that slowed transaction processing. One integrated, read-mostly copy served everyone without touching production.

choices.choice: Store data by column, not by row
choices.why: Row stores are optimised for writing whole records, which suits transactions. Warehouse queries aggregate a few columns over many rows, so storing each column together means reading far less data.
Appliances and shared-nothing clusters forced companies to buy for peak load and reshuffle data when resizing. Cloud warehouses keep data in shared storage and add compute on demand.

Devlin and Murphy at IBM describe the “business data warehouse”
Bill Inmon publishes Building the Data Warehouse

C-Store paper makes the case for column stores
Amazon Redshift launches, after BigQuery (2010); Snowflake follows
Lakehouse paper argues for warehouse features on open files
